chunks: Our response regarding the Imamate is like their response regarding the Knowledge (of God).

That the grace (of God) for the disbeliever remains present in the Knowledge (of God), but he has deprived himself through negligence in the contemplation that leads to it, so imposing duties upon him is not unjust.
Similarly, we say: The leadership (Imamate) is a grace for the duty-bound during the period of occultation.
And what pertains to God from His providing it is present/available.
But his administration and the extension of his hand have ceased due to a matter that returns to the duty-bound themselves, so the two matters (Imamate and Knowledge) have become equal.
And the discourse on this meaning is also complete, as we have mentioned it.

key_terms.الرِّيَاسَةُ: Leadership or headship, referring to the Imam's authority
key_terms.الْإِمَامَةِ: Imamate, the institution of divine leadership
key_terms.الْغَيْبَةِ: Occultation, the period of concealment of the Imam
key_terms.الْمَعْرِفَةِ: Knowledge, specifically gnosis or knowledge of God
key_terms.الْمُكَلَّفِينَ: The duty-bound, referring to the Muslim community responsible for religious duties

ai.seo_question: How does Shia theology justify the Imamate during the occultation if the Imam is not actively governing?
ai.summary: Al-Tusi employs the theological concept of 'lutf' (divine grace) to argue that the Imamate during the occultation remains a functional grace for the community, analogous to how knowledge of God remains available to the disbeliever despite their negligence. He clarifies that while the Imam's active governance and expansive authority are suspended due to divine decree, the essential reality of the Imamate persists, ensuring that the burden of attainment rests upon the believers' own actions rather than a defect in the Imam himself. This argument reinforces the Shia doctrine that the Imam's presence is ontologically necessary even when his political or juridical influence is latent.
